Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Maya, a 22‑year‑old South‑Asian delivery driver, recalled the night the mugging happened with a chilling clarity that still colors her everyday life. She was halfway across a quiet stretch of Main Street, bag in hand, when a group of men stepped out of a parked van and demanded her purse. The closest officer, a tall figure with a blue badge, marched into the scene, his presence a stark reminder of the authority that had previously forced her into compliance during the robbery. The sight of that officer, coupled with the uneasy feeling that people around her were suspiciously watching, triggered the same loss of autonomy she felt at the moment of the forced surrender. Those triggers made her feel trapped and compelled her to develop a series of maladaptive strategies: she stopped driving entirely, preferring to walk or walk on a bike, began taking pills to numb the panic, and would often tell herself, “I’m just imagining how bad it was,” to convince herself the event was less traumatic than it felt. The fear that the police were a permanent presence in her world reinforced her belief that she could never regain control, pushing her further into avoidance and numbing behaviors. The very triggers that started the spiral—being forced, police presence, suspicious crowds—also sparked her constant state of threat, as she now plans escape routes in the back of her mind before she can feel comfortable anywhere. She wakes every night to check whether the streetlights are on, whether a driver’s seat is still occupied, and whether her own heart rate is normal, never able to relax even when she knows she’s in a safe apartment. The mugging left a residue in Maya’s memory that is not a vivid picture but a collection of fragmented emotions. Sometimes she feels the full surge of terror—her chest tight, her hands shaking—without any clear image of the men’s faces. Other times, she hears the echo of the shouts and the metallic clank of the purse’s zipper in her own head, an auditory recall that flares up in the middle of a quiet room. Yet the most vivid detail is a snapshot of the moment the officer’s hand brushed her shoulder, the sudden realization that she was being observed, the freeze of a single breath that felt like a snapshot. These memories, whether they are just feelings, sounds, or brief images, ignite a sense of threat. As soon as the memory surfaces, Maya’s mind automatically begins to map out escape routes, to check if she can leave the scene quickly. The terror that arises from those memory fragments also fuels her negative appraisals; she thinks she should have resisted more, that she would never forgive herself for not doing anything else, and that this inability to stop the crime has left her helpless and isolated from those who might otherwise support her. Each time a memory surfaces, she feels the weight of guilt and helplessness more acutely, and her belief that she has no agency over her safety deepens. The guilt and helplessness that Maya carries as negative appraisals drive her toward more maladaptive strategies. She takes stronger doses of painkillers in the hopes of numbing the constant anxiety, but the pills only dull her sense of self, amplifying her feeling of isolation. Each dose feeds back into her sense of threat, because she knows the medication may fail when a real danger arises. Her belief that the threat is ever‑present pushes her to stay alert all the time; she keeps a phone with her at all moments, her eyes darting to see if someone is following, and her mind running through every possible escape scenario. The cycle of threat keeps her on edge, making it impossible to relax, even in a quiet, safe home. The constant sense of threat, in turn, reminds her of the triggers she experienced during the robbery. She fears the sight of any police officer, the presence of a stranger on the street, or a group of people who seem to watch her too closely. These triggers, re‑awakened by her heightened vigilance, reinforce the very threat she feels and keep her locked in a pattern of avoidance, medication use, and hypervigilance. Finally, Maya’s avoidance of driving is not only a reaction to the triggers but also a source of new triggers. By refusing to drive, she becomes dependent on walking or on rides from friends, which means she is often forced to negotiate with other people about transport. Each time she must rely on a stranger for a ride, she feels the same loss of autonomy she had during the robbery. The momentary feeling of being forced to comply with a taxi driver’s route or a friend’s schedule sparks the same anxiety, which in turn pushes her to seek more medication and avoid even the simplest journeys. The cycle feeds itself: avoidance strategies create triggers that lead back to threat, which then intensifies negative appraisals and memory recall, solidifying the spiral. It was the relentless, escalating anxiety and the fear that no one could keep her safe that finally pushed Maya to seek help. She is most afraid that the panic will finally overwhelm her in an ordinary delivery route, yet she also hopes that therapy can break this self‑reinforcing loop and restore a sense of control and safety.
